subChunks.title: Classical Mechanics — Forces, Motion & Momentum

storyBeats.txt: Newton's three laws fit on a single page, Theodora said. They are perhaps the most powerful single page in the history of science. From them follow the orbits of planets, the trajectory of every cannonball ever fired, and the engineering principles underlying every bridge and building ever constructed.

The genius of Newton was not just the laws themselves but the framework: that the same mathematics governs a falling apple and a falling moon. That celestial and terrestrial physics are one physics. Before Newton, they were thought to be separate domains.

Classical mechanics breaks down at very high speeds (special relativity takes over) and very small scales (quantum mechanics takes over). But for everyday speeds and everyday objects, Newton's laws predict the world with extraordinary precision.

subChunks.hookHtml: Classical mechanics — the branch of physics developed primarily by Galileo, Newton, and their contemporaries in the 17th century — describes the motion of objects under the action of forces. Despite being superseded at extreme scales by relativity and quantum mechanics, Newtonian mechanics remains the framework that engineers use to design bridges, that NASA uses to plan spacecraft trajectories, and that governs the motion of every object in everyday experience.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Kinematics — Describing Motion

Kinematics describes motion without reference to its causes. Key quantities:

  • Displacement (s): Change in position; vector (magnitude and direction).
  • Velocity (v): Rate of change of displacement; vector. v = Δs/Δt. Average vs instantaneous.
  • Acceleration (a): Rate of change of velocity; vector. a = Δv/Δt.
  • Speed: Magnitude of velocity; scalar.

Equations of motion (uniform acceleration only — SUVAT equations):

  • v = u + at
  • s = ut + ½at²
  • v² = u² + 2as
  • s = ½(u+v)t

where u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, s = displacement, t = time.

Projectile motion: motion under gravity alone (vertical acceleration g = 9.81 m/s², horizontal acceleration = 0). Horizontal and vertical components are independent. Time of flight determined by vertical motion; horizontal range by horizontal velocity × time of flight.

Newton's Laws of Motion

First Law (Law of Inertia): An object at rest remains at rest, and an object in uniform motion remains in uniform motion, unless acted upon by a net external force. Inertia is the resistance to change in motion — proportional to mass.

Second Law: The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: F = ma. (More precisely, F = dp/dt — force equals rate of change of momentum.) Units: newtons (N = kg·m·s⁻²). Direction of acceleration is same as direction of net force.

Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Forces always occur in pairs acting on different objects. A book rests on a table: the book exerts a force downward on the table (weight); the table exerts an equal force upward on the book (normal reaction). Note: action-reaction pairs act on different objects and never cancel.

Forces

  • Weight (W = mg): Gravitational force on an object. g = 9.81 m/s² near Earth's surface.
  • Normal force (N): Perpendicular contact force from a surface. Reaction to weight when on a horizontal surface.
  • Friction: Opposes relative motion or tendency to slide. Static friction (prevents motion) up to a maximum; kinetic friction (during sliding) = μₖN.
  • Tension: Force transmitted through a string/rope/cable.
  • Drag/air resistance: Opposes motion through a fluid; increases with speed.

Free body diagrams: isolate the object, draw all forces acting on it as vectors with magnitude and direction labelled. Sum forces in each direction (Newton's 2nd Law) to find net force and acceleration.

Momentum and Impulse

Linear momentum: p = mv (vector; SI unit: kg·m·s⁻¹). Newton's 2nd Law in momentum form: F = Δp/Δt.

Impulse: J = FΔt = Δp. Impulse equals change in momentum — a force applied over a time interval changes momentum. Airbags work by increasing collision time, reducing peak force (same Δp over longer Δt → smaller F).

Conservation of linear momentum: In a closed system (no external net force), total momentum is conserved. For a collision: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂. Types of collision:

  • Elastic: Both momentum and kinetic energy conserved. (Rare in practice — billiard balls approach this.)
  • Inelastic: Momentum conserved; kinetic energy not (some converted to heat/deformation). All real collisions.
  • Perfectly inelastic: Objects stick together after collision; maximum KE loss consistent with momentum conservation.

Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation

Every mass attracts every other mass: F = Gm₁m₂/r², where G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²·kg⁻² is the gravitational constant, m₁ and m₂ are the masses, and r is the distance between their centres. This law gives orbital mechanics: for circular orbits, gravitational force provides centripetal acceleration: Gm_planet/r² = v²/r = (4π²r)/T².

Kepler's Third Law (derived from Newton): T² ∝ r³ — the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its semi-major axis.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why airbags save lives using the concept of impulse and momentum — and why hitting a thick mattress hurts less than hitting a concrete wall at the same speed.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A car of mass 1,200 kg travelling at 20 m/s rear-ends a stationary van of mass 2,400 kg. They stick together after the collision. (1) Calculate the velocity of the combined wreckage immediately after the collision. (2) Calculate the kinetic energy before and after the collision, and state what happened to the 'lost' energy. (3) The collision lasts 0.15 seconds. Calculate the average force experienced by the car during the collision. (4) The driver of the car (mass 75 kg) wears a seatbelt that extends 0.30 m during the collision. Estimate the force the seatbelt exerts on the driver, assuming constant deceleration. (5) Would an airbag, which extends the stopping time to 0.25 s, reduce this force? Show a calculation.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Conservation of momentum: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁+m₂)v. 1200×20 + 2400×0 = (1200+2400)v. 24,000 = 3600v. v = 6.67 m/s (≈ 6.7 m/s).

(2) KE before = ½×1200×20² = ½×1200×400 = 240,000 J. KE after = ½×3600×6.67² = ½×3600×44.5 = 80,100 J. KE lost = 240,000 − 80,100 = 159,900 J ≈ 160 kJ. This energy is converted to heat (deformation of metal, tyre friction), sound, and light (sparks) — energy is conserved overall, but KE is not in inelastic collisions.

(3) The car changes momentum from 1200×20 = 24,000 kg·m/s to 1200×6.67 = 8,004 kg·m/s. Δp = 8004 − 24000 = −15,996 kg·m/s. F = Δp/Δt = 15,996/0.15 = 106,640 N ≈ 107 kN. (Force is negative/opposing; magnitude shown.)

(4) Driver decelerates from 20 m/s to 6.67 m/s. Using v² = u² + 2as: (6.67)² = (20)² + 2a(0.30). 44.5 = 400 + 0.6a. a = (44.5−400)/0.6 = −592 m/s². Force = ma = 75×592 = 44,400 N ≈ 44 kN. (Note: this is the net force; actual seatbelt force is slightly greater to overcome gravity.)

(5) With airbag: stopping time ≈ 0.25 s (from 20 to 6.67 m/s). F = mΔv/Δt = 75×(20−6.67)/0.25 = 75×13.33/0.25 = 4,000 N. The airbag reduces the force on the driver from ~44 kN (seatbelt alone, 0.15 s deceleration) to ~4 kN (airbag, 0.25 s). This is a factor of ~11 reduction, dramatically lowering the risk of chest and head injuries. The same change in momentum (same Δp = impulse) occurs over a much longer time, requiring much smaller average force.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A satellite orbits Earth in a circular orbit at an altitude of 400 km above the surface. (Earth's radius = 6,371 km; Earth's mass = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg; G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²·kg⁻².) (1) Calculate the orbital radius (distance from Earth's centre). (2) Calculate the orbital speed of the satellite. (3) Calculate the orbital period in minutes. (4) Explain why an astronaut in this satellite feels 'weightless' even though gravity is still acting on them — and why this is technically called 'microgravity' rather than 'zero gravity'.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Orbital radius r = Earth's radius + altitude = 6,371 + 400 = 6,771 km = 6.771 × 10⁶ m.

(2) For circular orbit, gravitational force = centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r. Cancel m: GM/r² = v²/r. v² = GM/r = (6.674×10⁻¹¹ × 5.97×10²⁴) / 6.771×10⁶ = (3.984×10¹⁴) / (6.771×10⁶) = 5.884×10⁷ m²/s². v = √(5.884×10⁷) = 7,671 m/s ≈ 7.67 km/s.

(3) Circumference = 2πr = 2π × 6.771×10⁶ = 4.253×10⁷ m. Period T = circumference/v = 4.253×10⁷ / 7,671 = 5,545 s = 92.4 minutes. (The ISS, at ~408 km altitude, orbits every ~92 minutes — consistent.)

(4) The astronaut feels weightless not because gravity is absent but because both the astronaut and the satellite are in free fall together around Earth. Gravity is providing the centripetal acceleration (g at 400 km altitude ≈ 8.7 m/s², only slightly less than surface g = 9.81 m/s²). In free fall, there is no normal force between the astronaut and the satellite floor — the floor accelerates downward (toward Earth) at the same rate as the astronaut, so they never push against each other. This is identical to the 'weightlessness' felt in a falling lift. It is called microgravity rather than zero gravity because: (a) gravity is not zero (it's ~89% of surface strength at this altitude); (b) there are tiny residual accelerations from tidal forces, atmospheric drag, and the non-uniform distribution of Earth's mass that produce small net forces — hence 'micro' rather than 'zero'.
learningObjectives: Apply the SUVAT equations to solve problems involving uniform acceleration, including projectile motion.
State Newton's three laws of motion and apply them to analyse forces on objects in equilibrium and in accelerated motion.
Apply conservation of linear momentum to elastic and inelastic collision problems, calculating post-collision velocities.
Derive orbital speed and period from Newton's law of universal gravitation and the condition for circular orbital motion.
commonMistakes: Applying SUVAT equations to non-uniform acceleration — SUVAT requires constant acceleration; for variable acceleration, calculus (integration) is needed.
Forgetting that Newton's Third Law pairs act on different objects — the weight of a book and the normal force from the table both act on the book, so they are NOT a Newton's Third Law pair.
Treating momentum conservation as applying to single objects — it applies to the total momentum of a system; individual objects can change momentum if a force acts on them.
Confusing mass and weight — mass (kg) is a measure of inertia; weight (N) is the gravitational force on that mass (W = mg).
assessmentCriteria: Correctly applies SUVAT equations to find unknown quantities in constant-acceleration scenarios with appropriate units.
Draws accurate free body diagrams and applies Newton's Second Law to find net force and acceleration.
Applies momentum conservation correctly to perfectly inelastic collisions and calculates energy loss.
Calculates orbital speed and period using gravitational and centripetal force balance, and explains microgravity correctly.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A reference frame in which Newton's First Law holds — a frame that is not accelerating. Newton's laws apply in inertial frames; in non-inertial (accelerating) frames, pseudo-forces (like the Coriolis force) must be introduced.

The mass-weighted average position of all particles in a system — the point at which the entire mass can be considered to act for calculating translational motion. For a uniform sphere, it is the geometric centre.

Elastic: both momentum and kinetic energy conserved. Inelastic: only momentum conserved; KE is partly converted to heat and deformation. Perfectly elastic collisions occur only between fundamental particles; real macroscopic collisions are always inelastic to some degree.

The constant velocity reached when drag force equals weight — net force is zero, so acceleration is zero. Objects falling through air approach terminal velocity; skydivers reach ~55 m/s belly-down, ~90 m/s head-down.

T² ∝ r³ — derived by Newton from his law of gravitation and the condition for circular orbits. The orbital period squared is proportional to the orbital radius cubed; allows calculation of orbital periods from distance and vice versa.

questions.questionHtml: A ball is thrown horizontally from a cliff at 15 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, how far has the ball fallen vertically after 3 seconds?
questions.explanationHtml: Vertical motion is independent of horizontal. Vertical: u = 0 (thrown horizontally, no initial vertical velocity), a = g = 10 m/s², t = 3 s. s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½×10×9 = 45 m. Note: horizontal velocity (15 m/s) has no effect on vertical fall distance — horizontal and vertical components are independent in projectile motion.

questions.questionHtml: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides and sticks to a stationary 5 kg trolley. What is their combined velocity after the collision?
options: 4 m/s — momentum is conserved so the velocity doesn't change
1.5 m/s — calculated using conservation of momentum
2.4 m/s — calculated using conservation of kinetic energy
questions.correctAnswer: 1.5 m/s — calculated using conservation of momentum
questions.explanationHtml: Conservation of momentum: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁+m₂)v. 3×4 + 5×0 = (3+5)v. 12 = 8v. v = 1.5 m/s. This is a perfectly inelastic collision (they stick together); KE is not conserved. KE before = ½×3×16 = 24 J; KE after = ½×8×2.25 = 9 J; 15 J converted to heat/deformation.

questions.questionHtml: A book rests on a table. The table exerts an upward normal force on the book equal in magnitude to the book's weight. Is this an example of Newton's Third Law, and why or why not?
options: Yes — equal and opposite forces are always a Newton's Third Law pair

No — Newton's Third Law pairs act on different objects. The weight (gravitational force on book from Earth) and normal force (contact force on book from table) both act on the book, so they are a Newton's First Law balance (equilibrium), not a Third Law pair. The Third Law pairs are: book's weight ↔ Earth's gravitational attraction to book (on Earth); normal force on book ↔ book's force downward on table
Yes — they are equal and opposite, and that is the definition of Newton's Third Law
No — Newton's Third Law only applies to objects in motion
questions.correctAnswer: No — Newton's Third Law pairs act on different objects. The weight (gravitational force on book from Earth) and normal force (contact force on book from table) both act on the book, so they are a Newton's First Law balance (equilibrium), not a Third Law pair. The Third Law pairs are: book's weight ↔ Earth's gravitational attraction to book (on Earth); normal force on book ↔ book's force downward on table
questions.explanationHtml: This is a classic misconception. Newton's Third Law states that force pairs act on different objects — specifically, when object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal and opposite force on object A. Weight and normal force BOTH act on the book (same object) — they are a Newton's First Law balance (the book is in equilibrium). The actual Third Law pairs: (1) Earth pulls book down (weight) ↔ book pulls Earth up gravitationally; (2) Table pushes book up (normal) ↔ book pushes table down. These pairs act on different objects.
